1.pericope_label: They that trust in the Lord shall be as mount Zion: as the mountains are round about Jerusalem

schools.summary: Augustine argues from the emptying of the earthly city that another Jerusalem must be meant, since one may now seek a Jew there and not find him, and holds that those who dwelt in the earthly one were moved first in heart and then by exile, casting their King outside the walls and being cast out of his city in turn.

Calvin asks not what the mountains are but why they are shown, holding them exhibited as a mirror to those who cannot apprehend the secret protection of God by faith, the prophet accommodating himself to men detained by the dulness of the flesh; Gill assembles ancient descriptions of the city and then turns the figure against itself with a Jewish commentator’s note that the mountains did not prevent its capture.

Spurgeon insists the blessing belongs not to some who trust but to all, calls trust in the living God sanctified common sense, and finds the Hebrew saying of the hill that it sits to eternity, neither bowing down nor moving to and fro; Henry makes trust the condition, since all who deal with God must deal upon trust and the closer expectation is confined to him the higher it may be raised.

Clarke notes the psalm has no title, dates it after the captivity, applies it to the opposition of Sanballat, Geshem and Tobiah during the rebuilding of the walls, quotes a traveller’s description of the city set as if in an amphitheatre of hills, and concludes that the situation could easily be made impregnable.

Ellicott quotes a modern survey to the effect that all the surrounding hills are higher than the city, and observes that a prophet elsewhere likens the same protection to a wall rather than to a rampart of mountains; Keil and Delitzsch date the psalm among the latest on the evidence of three late expressions, read the situation as foreign dominion tempting to apostasy, and set the encompassing God above the encompassing hills.

debates: Does the ring of mountains prove the point it is used for? Clarke concludes from a traveller’s description that the situation could easily be rendered impregnable; Gill reports a Jewish commentator observing that the mountains did not in fact hinder the enemy from taking the city, and infers that the Lord is a greater security than they were; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion without the objection, that there are mountains round Jerusalem but more important still is the God who encompasses his people; Calvin sets the survey aside and asks why the image is given at all, answering that it is a mirror held up to those who cannot grasp the protection of God by faith.

Which Jerusalem is promised permanence? Augustine argues from fact that it cannot be the earthly one, since all who dwelt there have been removed by wars and by the destruction of the city and a Jew is no longer to be found in it, so that another and heavenly city must be meant; the others read the verse of the church or of the believer without raising the question.
outliers: Gill supports the description of the city from a Roman historian who called it inaccessible for walls, mountains, rocks and towers, and from a Greek poet who mentioned a people speaking the Phoenician tongue who inhabited the mountains of Solyma, a name he traces to Homer and thence to the city’s own.
Calvin explains the visible image as an accommodation to the rudeness of those still detained by the dulness of the flesh and settled down in the earth.
Spurgeon renders the Hebrew of the hill as sitting to eternity, neither bowing down nor moving to and fro.
themes: trust rather than merit named as the condition
a city defended by hills that did not save it
a visible image offered as an accommodation to weak faith
an earthly promise transferred to a heavenly city
a psalm dated by the shape of its phrases

3.pericope_label: For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous: do good, O Lord, unto those that be good

schools.summary: Henry marks that the petition asks good not for the perfect and spotless but for the sincere and honest, so that those who are as they should be shall be as they would be; he traces the danger of the third verse to men driven into indirect courses under pressure, distinguishes predicting the ruin of deserters from praying for it, and observes that sinful ways are called crooked because sin is the perverting of what is right.

Gill canvasses the rod as correction, as a sceptre standing for the nations or the antichristian states, and as a tribe, reports the lot read either as the city or as the people who inherit the land, notes a Jewish commentator allowing the fourth verse to be prayer or prophecy, and takes the deserters of the last verse to be not open sinners but professors offended by persecution.

Clarke attacks the liturgical rendering of the third verse as neither truth nor scripture, calls the whole psalter of that book unworthy of regard and asks the bishops of his day to remove it, holds that religion would soon become extinct if the wicked bore rule in the Lord’s vineyard, and closes by making the judgment on deserters the purification of the church; Wesley reads the rod as power and authority and the danger as men driven to indirect courses to relieve themselves.

Ellicott identifies the rod as the heathen sceptre and notes that the verb rendered rest expresses the presence of tyranny, holding that God will not let it last lest the righteous be forced into connivance with what religion and patriotism unite to condemn; Keil and Delitzsch make the duration of the calamity exactly proportioned to the power of resistance of the righteous, and relay a rabbinic riddle on the fourth verse.

debates: Why is the rule of the wicked limited? Ellicott holds that God will not suffer it to last lest the righteous be seduced or forced into connivance with practices which religion and patriotism unite to condemn; Keil and Delitzsch make it a proportion instead, the duration of the calamity being exactly measured against the power of resistance of the righteous, whom God proves and purifies by it; Clarke puts the danger institutionally, that religion would soon become extinct if the wicked bore rule in the Lord’s vineyard; Wesley and Henry put it personally, that men under pressure are driven to indirect courses to relieve themselves.

Is the fourth verse a prayer or a prophecy? Gill reports a Jewish commentator allowing either; Henry treats it as prayer and notes that it asks good not for the perfect but for the sincere; Keil and Delitzsch read the whole as a petition arising out of the faith of the first verse and the hope of the third.
outliers: Clarke quotes an older writer dismissing the liturgical rendering of the third verse as neither truth nor scripture, since the rod of the wicked does often come into the inheritance of the righteous, and the text says only that it shall not rest there; Clarke then calls that whole version of the psalms unworthy of regard and asks the learned prelates of his day why they do not remove so sore a stumbling-block from the people.
Keil and Delitzsch relay a rabbinic riddle on the fourth verse, that a good one received a good thing from the good One for the good ones.
Henry distinguishes predicting the ruin of the deserters from praying for it, denying that he has desired the woeful day.
themes: oppression permitted but not allowed to settle
a translation attacked as neither true nor scriptural
the length of a trial measured by the strength to bear it
goodness asked for the sincere rather than the spotless
apostates counted with open workers of iniquity
